title: Pelvic floor exercises and vaginal pessaries for prolapse
intro: When pelvic organs such as the bladder, womb or bowel sag into the vagina, this is called prolapse. Pelvic floor exercises can reduce symptoms and may prevent it from worsening, and a vaginal pessary can support the organs without surgery. Both are options before or instead of an operation.

sections.heading: Understanding prolapse
paragraphs: Prolapse arises when the muscles and connective tissue supporting the pelvic organs weaken, often after childbirth, with age and menopause, or because of chronic straining or heavy lifting. Symptoms include a feeling of heaviness or a bulge in the vagina, urinary problems, difficulty emptying the bowel and discomfort during sex.

sections.heading: Pelvic floor muscle training
paragraphs: Supervised exercise programmes, usually led by a physiotherapist, can improve symptoms and sometimes the degree of prolapse in mild to moderate cases. The exercises involve repeated, strong contractions held for several seconds, practised daily for at least three months. Combine exercises with avoiding constipation and heavy lifting.

sections.heading: Vaginal pessaries
paragraphs: A pessary is a ring or other shaped device made of silicone that is placed in the vagina to support the organs. It can be fitted at a clinic in different sizes and shapes, and some women learn to insert and remove it themselves. Many women notice that symptoms improve quickly. Pessaries can be used for a long time or until surgery.

sections.heading: Possible problems
paragraphs: Possible issues include vaginal discharge, irritation, odour, spotting, difficulty passing urine or discomfort. It may need to be changed regularly. Vaginal oestrogen cream helps protect the vaginal skin after menopause. Report pain, bleeding or if the pessary falls out. Regular check-ups are needed, usually every few months, to inspect the skin.

sections.heading: Choosing between options
paragraphs: Exercises and pessaries are low-risk, and can be used together. Surgery may be considered if symptoms persist, but it also carries risks and the prolapse may return. Think about your goals, sexual activity, other health conditions and willingness to manage a device.

examples.title: Trying a pessary
examples.text: Imagine you feel a bulge and heaviness at the end of the day. You could ask a gynaecologist about a pessary fitting trial and learn how to care for it.

examples.title: Combining measures
examples.text: Suppose you have a pessary and want to improve muscle strength. You might see a pelvic floor physiotherapist to start a training programme and discuss lifting and constipation habits.
